newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr losing grip as rate tension climbs.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr losing grip as rate tension climbs.

text.p: The Australian dollar kept a fingertip hold on 75 cents in a sparse Monday session but the lack of any reply to last week's losses left sentiment bearish.
Traders reported bids at US$0.7505, partly exporter and options-related, while offers from offshore sources such as Swiss and New York investment banks were lurking at US$0.7530.

Interest differentials weighed against the dollar as the money market priced in another cut in official rates, so making it expensive to hold the A$ compared to the US$. The technical outlook had also taken a turn for the worse with the break of US$0.7550 support leaving analysts looking for US$0.7480 soon.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local currency was hovering at US$0.7513/18 having spent the entire day in a frustrating five tick range after lapsing from Friday's US$0.7524/29 finish.
It was mixed on the crosses, mirroring an indecisive performance by the U.S. dollar, at 85.75/95 yen from 85.90/00 late Friday and 1.3058/75 marks from 1.2987/00.
In trade weighted terms it was steady at 57.1.

The dollar sank a cent to plumb 16-month depths at US$0.7505 last week after shockingly poor employment data fanned fears the Reserve Bank could yet ease again. The currency had been testing the water atop 78 cents before the bank's last cut on May 23.

Most analysts reckoned the central bank would wait for its next monthly board meeting on July 1 to consider the matter given there was little domestic data out in the meantime and the U.S. Federal Reserve held a vital policy meeting on July 1-2.

Such logic was cold comfort to a market which has been badly caught out by three of the four rate cuts this cycle and traders were resigned to remaining on alert ahead of each and every RBA morning operation from now on.
The money market certainly thought it a foregone conclusion with the September 90-day bank bill contract up at 94.93 after rallying more than 1/4 point last week.

That implied a rate of 5.07 percent against the present cash rate of 5.50 percent. In contrast the three month Eurodollar contract was at 94.140 implying the market expected at least a 0.25 point hike in Fed fund rates from their 5.50 percent level.

This crossover in futures was a novel experience for most investors as A$ rates have traditionally traded well above their U.S. counterparts and the currency has long been pigeon-holed as a "high yielder" by offshore investors.
That was not to say the transformation was undeserved, given Australian inflation had averaged less than that in the U.S. for almost all the 1990's, analysts said.
This was being reflected in yield spreads between Australia and U.S. 10-year bonds which had shrunk to barely 50 basis points, a level not seen since 1983.
Inflation here was also set to slow further, particularly on the consumer price index where falling mortgage rates could take it comfortably under 1.0 percent later this year.
The latest reading in the U.S. put annual CPI at 2.4 percent and a tight labour market threatened to eventually push it higher, although up to now pressures had been remarkably light.
Indeed, U.S. producer price data Friday showed a surprise 0.3 percent fall in May emphasising the lack of immediate risk.
The data even made less likely the Fed would hike at its next meeting in July which in normal times would be bullish for the A$.
However, in this case it was a two-edged sword since the absence of a U.S. tightening could make the RBA more comfortable about easing soon.
The same was likely to be true of U.S. consumer price data Tuesday if they also showed subdued pressures.
There was almost no domestic data of note this week with quarterly dwelling comencements on Tuesday largely of academic interest. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
